list.listitem: Patients with biceps tendonitis typically present with pain in the anterior shoulder. The pain is usually localized to the bicipital (intertubercular) groove, but can radiate down the arm to the hand or to the deltoid muscle. This radiation can make the pain difficult to distinguish from that of the rotator cuff, an impingement syndrome, or cervical disc problems. It is more common in patients who use the arm repetitively (especially overhead).

Tenderness of the bicipital groove is best examined with the arm in 10° of internal rotation. This position places the biceps tendon approximately 3 inches below the acromion. External rotation of the arm should move this tenderness laterally if the biceps tendon is involved. This "tenderness in motion" is a specific finding for bicipital pathology.
However, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the accuracy of physical tests for bicipital pathology.

Consider injection of 1% lidocaine, sodium bicarbonate (1 meq/ml or 8.4%), and a corticosteroid in patients with presumed biceps tendonitis who have not responded to the conservative measures of rest and NSAIDs.

A patient may have a feeling of locking, catching, or popping in the shoulder and this may indicate a SLAP (Superior Labral Anterior and Posterior) lesion where the biceps is disinserted proximally. These lesions usually occur after trauma such as a fall, repetitive overhead motion in athletes, or a direct blow to the shoulder. An injection of 1% lidocaine and sodium bicarbonate (1 meq/ml or 8.4%) of the biceps peritendinous sheath will remove the pain from the biceps tendon and aid the diagnosis.
Obtain informed consent (see section on possible complications). Consider using ultrasound guidance if available.

Use 1% lidocaine without a methylparabens preservative- patients allergic to para-amino benzoic acid (PABA) are allergic to methylparabens as well. Consider adding sodium bicarbonate (1 mEq/mL or 8.4%) to reduce the sting in the same syringe in a ratio of 90% of 1% lidocaine to 10% of sodium bicarbonate mixture (e.g. add 9 cc of the 1% lidocaine to 1 cc of the sodium bicarbonate). The solution will remain stable for up to 5-6 hours in the same syringe without precipitation.

Assemble a 10 cc syringe, 25 g and 21 or 22 g 1.5 inch needles, alcohol swabs, gloves (sterile or nonsterile), povidone-iodine solution or swabs, steroid solution: Celestone (betamethasone sodium phosphate and acetate) 6 mg/mL or Kenalog (triamcinolone acetonide) 40 mg/mL, a 2 x 2 gauze square, a hemostat, marking pen, and a band-aid.

There are 2 techniques, 1 needle and 2 needle. Two-needle technique: use a smaller gauge needle, for example, 25 g for the 1% lidocaine and sodium bicarbonate for the skin. A 21 or 22 g needle is used to inject more of the anesthetic and possibly a steroid. One-needle technique: use the 21 or 22 g needle for both injections.

Have your patient lie down in a supine position and sterilize the injection area. Externally rotate the arm and place the elbow in 90° of flexion to expose the bicipital groove. Mark the most tender point. Using the one-needle technique, insert the 21 or 22 g needle attached to the 10 cc syringe containing 9 cc of 1% lidocaine and 1 cc of sodium bicarbonate subcutaneously parallel to the bicipital groove and aspirate to ensure you are not in a blood vessel. Inject about 8 cc of the 1% lidocaine and sodium bicarbonate mixture in a fan-like pattern in and around the biceps tendon sheath.

For a steroid injection, anchor the 21 or 22 g needle position and depth with a hemostat placed between the needle and skin, have an assistant hold the hemostat in place, and remove the 10 cc syringe of 1% lidocaine and sodium bicarbonate.. Place the syringe full of corticosteroid on the needle and inject subcutaneously in a fan-like pattern. Avoid tendon rupture by not injecting directly into the tendon itself (see ). An alternative is to mix the 1% lidocaine, sodium bicarbonate, and steroid preparation together in one syringe, but you risk not giving the 1% lidocaine enough time to achieve adequate anesthesia.

After injecting the steroid solution, remove the syringe and replace it with the syringe of 1% lidocaine and sodium bicarbonate. Slowly withdraw the needle while injecting the remaining 1% lidocaine mixture. This will flush any remaining steroid solution out of the needle and may lessen the chance of skin depigmentation and/or atrophy.4 The most common adverse reaction to an injection is the patient having vasovagal syncope so be prepared for this possibility.

Apply a band-aid for the next 8 to 10 hours. Tell the patient the signs and symptoms of infection and have them call your office if an infection starts. Reexamine the patient after 15 to 20 minutes. Pain relief indicates that biceps tendonitis is present or there is subluxation or instability of the biceps tendon.

Emphasize that the patient rest the injected shoulder. Patients may also attempt to obtain pain relief if needed with cold or warm compresses, NSAIDs, and a trial of physical therapy. The injection is not a cure itself and needs to be used with other pain relief modalities. Have the patient call your office if he or she develops fever, chills, increased pain in the joint for more than 72 hours, and erythema over the joint so you can examine them and rule out infection. The patient may resume normal bathing immediately after the procedure.

Atrophy or depigmentation of the skin or fatty atrophy of subcutanous (SQ) tissue may occur if a steroid is used.4 This cannot be repaired so the best treatment is prevention and obtaining adequate informed consent beforehand. The infection rate is approximately 18 cases per 250,000 procedures (0.072%). If infection (usually Staphylococcus) does occur, it is managed best with an oral cephalosporin antibiotic like Keflex (cephalexin) for 7 to 10 days. Increased pain in the shoulder may occur if the patient has a steroid flare. Manage the pain with oral medications (NSAIDs and possibly narcotics) until the pain has resolved. If the pain has not resolved after 48 to 72 hours, reexamine the patient for a possible septic joint. An allergic reaction to the medications is extremely rare, and could range from hives to anaphylaxis. Make sure that a full code cart is near your procedure room. Injection into an artery or vein may occur. There is also the possibility of damage to articular cartilage or nearby nerves. Patients should be told that it may take 2 or 3 steroid injections to obtain adequate pain relief. The rule-of-thumb is 3 injections in 1 year, usually 3 months apart.
Common CPT billing codes: 20550 Injection: tendon sheath 20610 Aspiration, injection, and/or arthrocentesis of a major joint (eg, shoulder)
A patient with a job that involves heavy lifting should be placed on light duty for 3 weeks after an injection.

No nursing assistance is required unless you use a hemostat to stabilize the needle and require multiple syringe changes and/or the operator is much smaller than the patient in size and assistances is needed should the patient have vasavagal syncope, is not lying supine, and is at risk of falling onto the floor.Injections of platelet-rich plasma have been not been proven beneficial for nonoperative treatment of rotator cuff disease.,
